newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian leader apologises to victims of Communism.
newsitem.headline: Romanian leader apologises to victims of Communism.

text.p: Romania's reformist president apologised on Friday for the horrors of Communist-era repression, in the first act of contrition by a Romanian leader since Communism's fall in 1989.

"In the name of the Romanian state, I ask for forgiveness from all the victims of Communist repression, be they known or unknown, dead or still alive," Emil Constantinescu said in a message sent to the opening of a three-day seminar in this northern Romanian town.
Constantinescu, who ousted an ex-Communist at polls last year, has vowed to help to heal the scars left on his nation by one of East Europe's most repressive Communist regimes.
"The only way to atone for keeping silent when they (Communism's victims) had the courage to speak out is to ask for their forgiveness now, when we are finally free," Constantinescu said.

His message moved many former political prisoners attending the conference on the horrors of Communist-era detention camps after 1947, when Romanians and fellow east Europeans were isolated behind the Iron Curtain.

Historians, political analysts and former dissidents from Romania, Albania, Slovakia, Russia, ex-Soviet Ukraine and Moldova are attending the event in former Sighetu Marmartiei jail, now a memorial to the victims of the Communist era.

Constantinescu urged parliament, dominated by centrists who ended the leftists' seven-year grip on power in last November's polls, to rehabilitate all the Romanians detained for their political beliefs.
"I ask parliament to initiate a law to pardon and quash all political sentences issued from 1948 to 1989, to redress what can be redressed after this disaster," his message said.

Former political prisoners' groups say some two million Romanians -- politicians, priests, army officers, farmers and students -- were jailed or detained in labour camps by the Communists who seized power in Romania after World War Two.

Romanian Foreign Minister Adrian Severin apologised to his German opposite number Klaus Kinkel last month for the deportation of thousands of ethnic Germans, sent by Romania's Moscow-backed Communists to Soviet slave labour camps.

"I was arrested at fifteen because I was caught spreading anti-Communist leaflets," one elderly woman said, tears welling up her eyes as she tried to identify familiar faces among the pictures of former inmates lining the fresh-painted walls of the former Sighetu Marmatiei jail.
The three-storey 19th century building in the town centre is the most notorious of Romania's 126 jails and labour camps where the ousted Communists held their political opponents.
It was dubbed "the prison for the elite" because 184 political leaders, senior clerics and high-ranking army officers died there without trial during the 1950s.

The Association of Former Political Prisoners (AFDPR) claims that as many as 200,000 Romanians died in prisons before 1964, when former ruler Nicolae Ceausescu released many opponents from jail but kept them under strict police surveillance.
"Our reconciliation must stand on truth and on repentance. We must begin with an act of justice to able to look into each other's eyes with no remorse," Constantinescu said.

Unlike Constantinescu, his predecessor Ion Iliescu, a former Communist who swept to power after Ceausescu was ousted and shot in a 1989 popular revolt, had failed to seek justice or to make amends for Communist-era crimes.
